Go around quickly. Model an honest, low-stakes word first, like scattered or relieved. The pause is the point. Pass is a full answer.

Louder or quieter, by thumbs. Next slide shows the answer. A student may say naming makes it bigger; the research points the other way.

Slide 5 · Notes

Psychologists call it emotional granularity. People with more of it lash out and binge less when upset, and report less anxiety and depression. Your body often knows first: chest, stomach, jaw, shoulders.

Slide 6 · Notes

Adapted from Nonviolent Communication; self-determination theory puts autonomy, competence and connection at the core. Quick pair: Connection met feels warm; not met feels lonely or hurt. Ask: which one do teenagers get the least of? Freedom usually comes up fast.

Thumbs up for a feeling, down for a thought in disguise. The test: if you can add “like” or “that” after “I feel,” it’s usually a thought.

Ask: what might be underneath “I feel like I’m not good enough”? Discouraged, embarrassed, scared.

A request is clear and doable: “Can we talk tonight instead of over text?” A request can get a no; if no isn’t allowed, it’s a demand. Most needs have more than one door. And name it before you open the app.

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Private; the card goes home. Add a request if they want one. Share the take-home link. A need for safety that isn’t met is a reason to talk to a counselor soon.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why putting a precise word to a feeling helps (naming turns the alarm down), connect a feeling to the need underneath it, and try the Feeling. Need. Request. steps on something small. Discussion stays on made-up characters; nobody has to share their own feelings.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minOne-word check-in
  2. 2 minNaming turns the alarm down, and go one past stressed
  3. 2 minSeven needs
  4. 3 minBetter words: turn and talk, share out
  5. 2 minFeeling, or a thought in disguise?
  6. 5 minName that need: Clara, Kai, Grace
  7. 3 minFeeling, need, request, and close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The check-in, naming turns the alarm down, one or two stories, and I feel ___ because I need ___.

Before you teach
Keep it on the characters.

Nobody should have to share their own feelings out loud. The stories are made-up students, not anyone in the room. If students disagree about the need, that's a good discussion: a feeling can come from more than one need.

Passing is always allowed.

In the check-in, "pass" is a full answer. Some students are having a hard week and don't want the circle to know. Move on without comment.

If a word in the check-in worries you.

If someone says "hopeless," "numb" or something heavier, don't stop the circle to ask about it. Check in privately afterward and connect them with a counselor that day. Don't ask screening questions in advisory.

Safety is a need too.

If a student says a need for safety isn't being met, at home, online or in a relationship, that goes to a counselor the same day.

Kai's story may be someone's life.

Some students translate for their families or help with bills. Don't look at anyone while reading it, and don't invite students to say it's them.

Grace's story can sting in the fall.

College conversations at home are tense for many seniors right now. Keep it on Grace, and treat both of her needs as real.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Feelings in more than one language.

Some students think about feelings in a language other than English, or have a family word that English doesn't. Say clearly that any language counts in the check-in and on the card. Kai's story makes room for students who interpret for their families.

Which feelings get said out loud varies.

The Tsai study shows that cultures value different feelings (excited versus calm), and families differ on which feelings get named and to whom. Avoid "In X families" generalizations. Ask students to notice their own home's rules, privately.

Naming feelings is harder for some brains.

Some autistic students, and others, find it hard to put feelings into words or notice body signals later. That's a difference to meet with patience. The word banks, the body check (chest, stomach, jaw, shoulders) and multiple-choice options help. Don't require eye contact in the circle.

Family structure.

Grace's parents are in her story, but say "parent or caregiver" when you talk about needs at home. Students live with grandparents, one parent, two moms or two dads, in foster or kinship care, or across two homes.

Rest isn't equally available.

Clara works weekends and Kai helps with bills. Some students can't just take a night off. When talking about the Body need, offer small, free options and avoid implying that rest is a choice everyone has.

Boys get to be hurt and lonely.

Students hear that some feelings belong to some genders. Mix genders when giving examples, and when a student offers "hurt" or "lonely" for Andre or Kai, treat it as an ordinary, accurate answer.

What the research says

Putting a word to the emotion in a face ("angry," "scared") turned down activity in the amygdala and turned up activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex. The two moved in opposite directions.

Lieberman et al., 2007, Psychological Science (UCLA)

People afraid of spiders who described their feelings out loud while near one had smaller physical fear responses a week later than people who distracted themselves or tried to talk themselves out of it.

Kircanski, Lieberman and Craske, 2012, Psychological Science

The insula tracks signals from inside the body (heartbeat, gut, breathing, muscle tension). Neuroscientist Bud Craig proposed it's where those signals become conscious feelings.

Craig, 2009, Nature Reviews Neuroscience

People who describe emotions in more detail (emotional granularity) are less likely to binge drink, lash out or hurt themselves when upset, and report less severe anxiety and depression.

Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight, 2015, Current Directions in Psychological Science

Self-determination theory points to three needs at the core of motivation and well-being: autonomy, competence and relatedness.

Ryan and Deci, 2000, American Psychologist

European American participants ideally wanted to feel excited more than Hong Kong Chinese participants, who valued calm more. Chinese American participants landed in between.

Tsai, Knutson and Fung, 2006, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Stanford)

The seven need categories and the feeling word banks are adapted from the Feelings Inventory and Needs Inventory.
